The model-merging contribution is technically incremental and lacks decisive baselines. Linear interpolation and SLERP are standard, while the paper omits joint training on the union or a controlled mixture of both datasets, candidate pooling from the two specialized models, and stronger merging methods. The evaluation does not establish statistical robustness. Results come from only 80 test problems but are reported over 1,422 potentially correlated program pairs, without counts of unique source programs, per-problem aggregation, confidence intervals, significance tests, or variation over fine-tuning and decoding seeds. Arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by outliers, and assigning speedup 1.0 to every incorrect or slower output hides regressions; distributions, medians/geometric means, and per-problem results are needed.

Passing a finite set averaging 104 tests per problem is treated as functional equivalence despite the aggressive algorithm changes being studied. No additional held-out, generated, adversarial, or formal correctness checks are used. Reproducibility is insufficient for the strength of the claims. The paper says that data, code, and evaluation scripts are public but provides no corresponding link.
